facts: Velocity is the derivative of position: $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)=\dot{x}(t)\underset{\sim}{i}+\dot{y}(t)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=\ddot{x}(t)\underset{\sim}{i}+\ddot{y}(t)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Differentiate the $\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ components separately, because $\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ are constant.
**Speed** is the size of the velocity, $|\underset{\sim}{v}|=\sqrt{\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}}$, so it is never negative.
Speed is not $\dot{x}+\dot{y}$: square the components, add, then take the square root.
When the velocity is non-zero, the velocity vector points along the tangent to the particle's path at that instant.
Velocity and acceleration need not point the same way; in circular motion at constant non-zero speed they are perpendicular.
To find velocity or acceleration at $t=a$, differentiate first and substitute afterwards.
steps: Write the components $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ of the position vector
Differentiate each component of $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$ to get $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$
Substitute the required value of $t$, and take a magnitude if speed is asked for

workedExamples.question_text: A particle's position in metres is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=3t^2\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^3+5t)\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t\geq0$ is measured in seconds. Find its velocity and acceleration vectors, then its velocity and speed at $t=1$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Differentiate each component separately.
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=\dfrac{d}{dt}(3t^2)\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{d}{dt}(t^3+5t)\underset{\sim}{j}\\&=6t\underset{\sim}{i}+(3t^2+5)\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{a}(t)&=6\underset{\sim}{i}+6t\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$
Velocity is measured in metres per second and acceleration in metres per second squared.
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(1)&=6\underset{\sim}{i}+8\underset{\sim}{j}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\\|\underset{\sim}{v}(1)|&=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}\\&=10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=e^{3t}\underset{\sim}{i}+\ln(2t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find its velocity and acceleration vectors.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Apply the chain rule to each component.
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=3e^{3t}\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{2}{2t+1}\underset{\sim}{j}\\\underset{\sim}{a}(t)&=9e^{3t}\underset{\sim}{i}-\dfrac{4}{(2t+1)^2}\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=te^{-2t}\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^2+3)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find its velocity at $t=0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Use the product rule for the first component.
$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}(t)&=e^{-2t}-2te^{-2t}\\\dot{y}(t)&=2t\\\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=(e^{-2t}-2te^{-2t})\underset{\sim}{i}+2t\underset{\sim}{j}\\\underset{\sim}{v}(0)&=(1-0)\underset{\sim}{i}+0\underset{\sim}{j}\\&=\underset{\sim}{i}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\dfrac{2t}{t+2}\underset{\sim}{i}+\sqrt{6t+1}\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find its velocity vector.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Use the quotient rule for the first component and the chain rule for the second.
$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}(t)&=\dfrac{2(t+2)-2t}{(t+2)^2}\\&=\dfrac{4}{(t+2)^2}\\\dot{y}(t)&=\dfrac{6}{2\sqrt{6t+1}}\\&=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{6t+1}}\\\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=\dfrac{4}{(t+2)^2}\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{6t+1}}\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: A particle's position in metres is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=3\cos(4t)\underset{\sim}{i}+3\sin(4t)\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t\geq0$ is measured in seconds and angles are in radians. Show that its speed is constant, that $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=-16\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$, and that its velocity and acceleration are perpendicular.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2t^3-9t^2)\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{t^4}{2}\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find its acceleration vector and the time when the first component of acceleration is zero. Is the entire acceleration vector zero then?
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=(6t^2-18t)\underset{\sim}{i}+2t^3\underset{\sim}{j}\\\underset{\sim}{a}(t)&=(12t-18)\underset{\sim}{i}+6t^2\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$
Set the first component equal to zero.
$\begin{aligned}12t-18&=0\\12t&=18\\t&=\dfrac32\end{aligned}$
$\underset{\sim}{a}\left(\dfrac32\right)=\dfrac{27}{2}\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Only the first component is zero; the acceleration vector is non-zero.

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2t^2+pt)\underset{\sim}{i}+qt^3\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Given $\underset{\sim}{v}(2)=11\underset{\sim}{i}+24\underset{\sim}{j}$, find $p$ and $q$.
A particle's position in metres is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^2-6t)\underset{\sim}{i}+4t\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t\geq0$ is measured in seconds. Find its minimum speed and when it occurs.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=(2t-6)\underset{\sim}{i}+4\underset{\sim}{j}\\|\underset{\sim}{v}(t)|^2&=(2t-6)^2+16\end{aligned}$
The square root is increasing, so minimise the squared speed. The squared term has minimum zero.
$\begin{aligned}2t-6&=0\\t&=3\end{aligned}$
This time is in the domain $t\geq0$.
$\begin{aligned}|\underset{\sim}{v}(3)|&=\sqrt{0+16}\\&=4\ \text{m s}^{-1}\end{aligned}$
The minimum speed is $4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $t=3\ \text{s}$.

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=e^t\cos(2t)\underset{\sim}{i}+e^t\sin(2t)\underset{\sim}{j}$. Show that $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=2\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-5\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Differentiate using the product and chain rules.
$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}(t)&=e^t\cos(2t)-2e^t\sin(2t)\\\dot{y}(t)&=e^t\sin(2t)+2e^t\cos(2t)\\\ddot{x}(t)&=e^t\cos(2t)-2e^t\sin(2t)-2e^t\sin(2t)-4e^t\cos(2t)\\&=-3e^t\cos(2t)-4e^t\sin(2t)\\\ddot{y}(t)&=e^t\sin(2t)+2e^t\cos(2t)+2e^t\cos(2t)-4e^t\sin(2t)\\&=-3e^t\sin(2t)+4e^t\cos(2t)\end{aligned}$
Now compare components of the required expression.
$\begin{aligned}2\dot{x}(t)-5x(t)&=2(e^t\cos(2t)-2e^t\sin(2t))-5e^t\cos(2t)\\&=-3e^t\cos(2t)-4e^t\sin(2t)\\&=\ddot{x}(t)\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}2\dot{y}(t)-5y(t)&=2(e^t\sin(2t)+2e^t\cos(2t))-5e^t\sin(2t)\\&=-3e^t\sin(2t)+4e^t\cos(2t)\\&=\ddot{y}(t)\end{aligned}$
Both components agree, so $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=2\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-5\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$.

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^2-10t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^2+4t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find when its velocity is parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)=(2t-10)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t+4)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
For parallel vectors, the second component must be twice the first.
$\begin{aligned}2t+4&=2(2t-10)\\2t+4&=4t-20\\24&=2t\\t&=12\end{aligned}$
Check the velocity is a non-zero scalar multiple of the given vector.
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(12)&=14\underset{\sim}{i}+28\underset{\sim}{j}\\&=14(\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j})\end{aligned}$
The required time is $t=12$.

development.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=3\cos 2t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+3\sin 2t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Find $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=e^{2t}\underset{\sim}{i}+\ln(t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge 0$.
Find $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=te^{-t}\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Find its velocity when $t=0$.

development.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$
$=-12\sin 3t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+12\cos 3t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$|\underset{\sim}{v}(t)|$
$=\sqrt{144\sin^{2}3t+144\cos^{2}3t}$
$=\sqrt{144(\sin^{2}3t+\cos^{2}3t)}$
$=\sqrt{144}$
$=12$
The speed does not depend on $t$, so it is constant at $12$.

development.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=2\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+2\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Show that $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$ and that $\underset{\sim}{a}$ is perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{v}$.
development.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$
$=-2\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+2\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$
$=-2\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}-2\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=-\left(2\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+2\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}\right)$
$=-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$
$\underset{\sim}{v}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}$
$=(-2\sin t)(-2\cos t)+(2\cos t)(-2\sin t)$
$=4\sin t\cos t-4\sin t\cos t$
$=0$
The dot product is zero, so $\underset{\sim}{a}$ is perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{v}$.

mastery.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}+at)\underset{\sim}{i}+bt^{3}\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants.
Given that $\underset{\sim}{v}(1)=5\underset{\sim}{i}+6\underset{\sim}{j}$, find $a$ and $b$.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-4t)\underset{\sim}{i}+3t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge 0$.
Find the minimum speed of the particle and the time at which it occurs.
mastery.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$
$=(2t-4)\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{j}$
$|\underset{\sim}{v}|^{2}$
$=(2t-4)^{2}+9$
The square root is increasing, so the speed is least when $(2t-4)^{2}$ is least.
$(2t-4)^{2}=0$
$t=2$
$|\underset{\sim}{v}(2)|$
$=\sqrt{0+9}$
$=3$
The minimum speed is $3$, at $t=2$.

mastery.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=e^{t}\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+e^{t}\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Show that $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=2\left(\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)\right)$.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dot{x}$
$=e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t$
$\dot{y}$
$=e^{t}\sin t+e^{t}\cos t$
$\ddot{x}$
$=(e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t)+(-e^{t}\sin t-e^{t}\cos t)$
$=-2e^{t}\sin t$
$\ddot{y}$
$=(e^{t}\sin t+e^{t}\cos t)+(e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t)$
$=2e^{t}\cos t$
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$
$=(e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t-e^{t}\cos t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(e^{t}\sin t+e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t)\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=-e^{t}\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+e^{t}\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$2\left(\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)\right)$
$=-2e^{t}\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+2e^{t}\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$
